title: How To Motivate Your Students To Behave Better, Work Harder, Care For Each Other… Or Anything Else You Want From Them
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes between individually lecturing a misbehaving student, which he calls a mistake driven by frustration that fails to change behavior, and delivering a structured, whole-class "motivational speech," which he presents as a powerful tool for shifting group attitude or effort. He lays out a five-step structure for such a speech: naming the unwanted behavior without singling anyone out, explaining clearly why it's wrong, describing the desired behavior in specific terms, challenging students who feel they can't meet the expectation to identify themselves, and closing with a physical, communal moment where committed students gather together and affirm the challenge out loud. He stresses that the technique only works if the teacher's own passion and belief in students' capability is genuine and visibly present, since a going-through-the-motions delivery will fall flat.
points: Individually lecturing a misbehaving student is framed as an ineffective habit born of frustration, unlike a structured whole-class "motivational speech."
A five-step speech structure moves from naming unwanted behavior, to explaining why it's wrong, to describing the desired behavior, to a group challenge and physical closing moment.
Explaining the reasoning behind an expectation is described as a powerful persuasion technique that increases buy-in.
The technique's effectiveness depends on the teacher's visible, genuine passion and belief in students' capability.
quotes: Lecturing individual students is a common classroom management practice—just another tool in a teacher’s tool belt. But it’s a colossal mistake, born of frustration, that does nothing to curb unwanted behavior beyond several minutes.
When you lecture individual students, it’s done out of anger and not out of a pure intention to help improve behavior. And students know it.
I prefer to call class lectures “motivational speeches” because that’s what they’re designed to do: to motivate students.
Explaining why is a powerful persuasion technique. Your students are much more likely to agree with you-and thus change their behavior-if you offer a clear explanation why their behavior is wrong.
Challenge your class to stand and gather around you if they are committed to whatever you’re asking of them.
You have to believe, to know beyond a doubt, that your students are capable of fulfilling the vision of excellence you have for them. Because if you don’t believe it, they won’t believe it either.
If you get goose bumps as you look into your students’ eyes, if they look back at you with intensity and determination to be better students, then you know you’re on the right track.
